gradient_descent: Gradient descent is the workhorse of machine learning. To minimize a loss, you compute its gradient with respect to the parameters and take a small step in the opposite direction, because the gradient points uphill. The size of that step is the learning rate. If the learning rate is too large the loss can bounce around or explode; if it is too small, training crawls. Stochastic gradient descent estimates the gradient from a random mini-batch instead of the whole dataset, which is noisier but far cheaper per step.
overfitting: A model overfits when it memorizes the training set instead of learning patterns that generalize. The telltale sign is a training loss that keeps falling while the validation loss starts rising. Common remedies are more data, data augmentation, a smaller model, weight decay (L2 regularization), dropout, and early stopping, which means halting training at the epoch with the best validation loss. Underfitting is the opposite problem: the model is too simple to capture the signal, so both losses stay high.
dropout: Dropout is a regularization technique for neural networks. During training, each activation is set to zero with probability p, and the surviving activations are scaled up by 1/(1-p) so their expected value is unchanged. This stops units from relying on specific partners and acts like training an ensemble of thinned networks. At test time dropout is switched off, which in PyTorch happens when you call model.eval().
adam: Adam is an optimizer that combines momentum with per-parameter adaptive learning rates. It keeps an exponential moving average of the gradients (the first moment) and of the squared gradients (the second moment), corrects both for their bias toward zero early in training, and divides the first by the square root of the second. Typical defaults are a learning rate of 0.001, beta1 of 0.9 and beta2 of 0.999. AdamW is a variant that applies weight decay directly to the weights instead of mixing it into the gradient.
cross_entropy: Cross-entropy loss measures how well a predicted probability distribution matches the true labels. For classification it is the negative log of the probability the model assigned to the correct class, averaged over examples. A confident correct prediction costs almost nothing, while a confident wrong one costs a lot. A model that guesses uniformly over V classes has a cross-entropy of ln(V), which is a useful sanity check at the start of training.
batch_norm: Batch normalization normalizes each feature using the mean and variance of the current mini-batch, then applies a learned scale (gamma) and shift (beta). It often lets you train deeper networks with higher learning rates. During training it uses batch statistics and updates running averages; at inference it uses those running averages instead. Transformers usually use layer normalization, which normalizes across the features of each example and does not depend on the batch.
attention: Self-attention lets every token in a sequence look at every other token. Each token is projected into a query, a key and a value. The attention weights are the softmax of the query-key dot products divided by the square root of the key dimension, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel on smaller projections. In a decoder, a causal mask hides future positions so the model cannot cheat when predicting the next token.
bpe: Byte-pair encoding (BPE) is the tokenization method used by GPT models. It starts with a vocabulary of the 256 possible bytes and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until it reaches the target vocabulary size. Frequent words end up as single tokens while rare words are split into pieces, so any text can be encoded without an unknown-token problem. Encoding new text replays the learned merges in the order they were learned.
lora: LoRA (low-rank adaptation) fine-tunes a large model by freezing its weights and learning a small low-rank update for selected layers. For a weight matrix W, the update is B times A scaled by alpha divided by r, where r is the rank. Matrix A is initialized randomly and matrix B is initialized to zero, so training starts from exactly the original model. Because only A and B are trained, LoRA cuts the number of trainable parameters by orders of magnitude, and the adapter can be merged back into W after training.
pca: Principal component analysis (PCA) reduces the dimensionality of data by projecting it onto the directions of greatest variance. Those directions, the principal components, are the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, and can be found with a singular value decomposition of the centered data. Keeping the first few components preserves most of the variance while dropping noise. PCA is linear and sensitive to feature scale, so features are usually standardized first.
kmeans: K-means clustering partitions data into k groups. It alternates two steps: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of the points assigned to it. It stops when the assignments no longer change. The result depends on the initial centroids, so it is common to run it several times or use the k-means++ initialization. The elbow method plots the within-cluster sum of squares against k to help choose the number of clusters.
q_learning: Q-learning is a reinforcement learning algorithm that learns the value of taking each action in each state. After every step it nudges Q(s, a) toward the reward plus the discount factor gamma times the best Q-value of the next state. To balance exploration and exploitation, an epsilon-greedy policy picks a random action with probability epsilon and the best known action otherwise. Q-learning is off-policy: it learns about the greedy policy while following a more exploratory one.
